## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pūtimukhapetavatthu* (Pv 3) is a text within the *Petavatthu* collection concerning the karmic consequences of verbal misconduct [SuttaCentral]. In the narrative, a hungry ghost explains the danger of harsh speech, lying, and slander [SuttaCentral; Shirker]. The ghost—a former monk who is encountered floating in mid-air by the elder Nārada—exhibits a striking contrast: while possessing a radiant, heavenly body, he is tormented by a worm-infested, foul-smelling mouth as retribution for his past slander [Shirker]. The peta implores Nārada that compassionate and skilled teachers should caution others never to engage in slander or falsehoods [Shirker]. The story's background involves two austere monks residing harmoniously in a village setting, touching upon the status of a *puthujjana* (an uninstructed worldling lacking the insight of noble disciples) [Shirker].
SuttaCentral notes five translations of the text in five modern languages, without recording any external parallels [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus identified no cross-language parallels with score ≥ 10, but found internal Pali text reuse spanning eight matching passages (709 characters, longest segment §0.3–1.4) shared with the commentary, the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
